title: The prayer rope
hookLine: a knotted wool rope, one Jesus Prayer per knot

cards: A loop of black wool sits in a monk's hand. It isn't a string of beads. It's knots, each one tied by hand, close together, with a small woolen cross where the loop closes.
His thumb finds a knot, and he says a short prayer. Then the next knot, another prayer. Nothing about it is fancy.
It would fit in a coat pocket. You met the Jesus Prayer back on day ninety-nine; this is the thing in the hand that keeps it company. In Greek it's called a komboskini.
In Russian it's chotki, and that's today's word.

teach.b: Why knots at all? Paul tells the Thessalonians, in three words, "Pray without ceasing." For anyone who takes that at its word, a rope helps: a way to keep going without losing your place, or your attention.
It's cheap, quiet and always to hand. There's a story about the knots. Tradition says a monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept coming in the night and untying them.

teach.h: A KNOT THE DEVIL COULDN'T UNTIE.
teach.b: So he was shown a new kind of knot, woven out of little crosses, that the devil couldn't undo. It's a legend, but it says plainly what the rope is for: a prayer, tied tight. The prayer itself is short.

Its usual form asks the Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, to have mercy on me, a sinner, and its words echo the Gospels. A blind man by the road at Jericho shouts, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me."
A tax collector in the temple won't even lift his eyes, and prays, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Put those two together and you can hear it.
And the rope isn't a scoreboard. In this tradition the point is attention, not the total. The knot under the thumb brings a wandering mind back, gently, the way a friend's hand on your shoulder does.
Lose your place, and you simply carry on from the next knot.

how: Orthodox monks and lay people pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted wool rope, moving the thumb one knot for each prayer; in Greek it is called a komboskini, in Russian chotki.

games.q: you're halfway around the prayer rope and realize your mind wandered and you've lost count. what do you do?
o: start the whole rope over, and get it perfect this time.
find the next knot and keep praying.
put it away and try again tomorrow.
games.why: the rope can help keep count, but the point is attention, not a perfect total. you pick up at the next knot and carry on.

practice: Tie a few knots, slowly, in whatever is at hand: a shoelace, a thread, a phone charger if that's all you've got.

Hold it and let your thumb find one knot at a time; if you pray, say the Jesus Prayer once for each, and if you don't, take one breath for each, a single moment of attention. When your mind wanders, the next knot calls you back.

wordCard.voice: Chotki. The Orthodox prayer rope: knotted wool, one Jesus Prayer for each knot, and a thumb that keeps the place.

orig.note: Russian for a prayer rope or prayer beads; in Greek the knotted rope is a κομποσκοίνι, komboskini.
